lobbying_activities.description: ACPs 2026 Third Quarter Lobbying Disclosure Report Medicare Payments to Physicians: Sent letter and met with legislators in support of the Patients First Act of 2026, (H.R. 9693) for a Medicare Economic Index inflationary updated to the physician fee schedule for physician practices, support for independent practices and replacement of MIPS with POINTS for quality measures. Supported and urged Congress to pass (H.R. 8163, S.5180), the Provider Reimbursement Stability Act, to enhance Medicare reimbursement stability for physicians by modernizing the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule. The Provider Reimbursement Stability Act of 2026. H.R. 8163 would raise the budget neutrality threshold from $20 million to $57.64 million and would use cumulative increases in the Medicare Economic Index (MEI) to update the threshold every 5 years. ACP supported the Medicare Physician Data-Drive Performance Payment System Act of 2026, H.R. 8622. This critical legislation seeks to modernize Medicare payments by reducing administrative burdens, improving patient care, and supporting small/rural practices through a more practical, data-driven approach. Dr. William Fox, Chair Emeritus of ACPs Board of Regents, testified before the House Energy and Commerce Committees Health Subcommittee on policy reforms to improve the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule and the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act (MACRA) on behalf of ACP. Dr. Rebecca Andrews, Past Chair of ACPs Board of Regents, testified before the House E&C Health Subcommittee in favor of each of the bills mentioned above. ACP supported Pay PCPs Act of 2026 (S. 5269), to inject $10 billion federal investment from fiscal year 2027 through 2031 to provide for the establishment of hybrid primary care payments under Medicare. Support Value-Based Care: Urged reintroduction and support of the Value in Health Care Act of 2024. The bill provides a multi-year commitment to reforming care delivery by extending MACRAs 5 percent advanced alternative payment models (APM) incentives that expired at the end of 2024. ACP supported the Preserving Patient Access to Accountable Care Act which aligns with Colleges policy to support the transition to value-based payments through alternative payment models (APMs) that can accommodate a wide range of specialties, practice sizes, and unique patient populations. ACP supported this legislation as it would extend the incentive payments for qualifying physicians and other clinicians to participate in Medicare advanced APMs through payment year 2027 at an increased amount of 3.53 percent and would freeze the scheduled increase in qualifying thresholds. Pricing Transparency/Consolidation: Provided comments to the House Energy and Commerce Committees markup, which includes the Lower Cost, More Transparency Act, H.R. 9393, and the Improving Seniors Timely Access to Care Act, H.R. 3514. The two bills would enhance price transparency across health care entities and streamline unnecessary administrative burden, respectively. ACP also supported several policies included in bills slated for markup that would reform Medicare Advantage practices to ensure accountability and safeguard market competition. ACP strongly supports pricing transparency in health care. ACP supported the passage of the Lower Costs, More Transparency Act, which passed the House in the 118th Congress, and we continue to support its reintroduction and passage in this Congress under H.R. 9393. ACP supported provisions within the Medicare Advantage Cost Transparency Act, H.R. 9392, led by Ranking Member DeGette and Dr. Joyce, which would provide greater oversight by requiring that Medicare Advantage (MA) plans report to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) on encounter data, including the allowed amount that a plan agreed to pay for a service in total and the total out-of-pocket costs the patient pays for a service. The College has repeatedly voiced support for the Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act, led by Reps. Kelly and DelBene, which would protect patients from unnecessary delays in care and reduce administrative burden on physicians by streamlining MAs prior authorization approval processes. We urge Congress to pass H.R. 3514 to ensure that our patients will get the care they need, when they need it most. FY2026 Appropriations/Agency Restructuring: For FY2027, ACP is urged appropriations committees that funding be either maintained or increased for the following proven programs: 1) Health Resources Services Administration (HRSA), $10.5 billion, including: 2) Health Workforce, National Health Service Corps (NHSC), $915.6 million in total program funding; 3) Primary Care Training and Enhancement (PCTE), $71 million; 4) Title X Family Planning Program, $390 million; 5) Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), $500 million; 6) Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) Injury Prevention and Control, $11.6 billion, including: 7) Firearm Injury and Mortality Prevention Research, $35 million; 8) Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion, Social Determinants of Health, $100 million; 9) National Institutes of Health (NIH), $51.3 billion, including: 10) Office of the Director, Firearms Research, $25 million; 11) Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) and Government Accountability Office (GAO); and 12) Report language to ensure primary care physicians are receiving Medicare physician revaluations. We urged Congress to include report language in the FY2026 Labor HHS appropriations bill to direct the GAO to conduct a study encompassing the last decade of CMS estimates of new and revised code utilizations. ACP believes CMS has overestimated utilizations, thus adversely affecting available funds in the Medicare physician fee schedule for other code usage. While the House and Senate bills included language, we prefer the stronger House version language and hope Congress will pass the FY26 Labor HHS bills. Also urged Congress to include report language in the FY2027 Labor HHS appropriations bill directing a study on extent G2211 add on codes and increases in fee schedule for primary care are being retained by hiring entities (hospitals, ACOs, private equity) versus the physicians. ACP urged appropriators to provide $35 million for the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), $25 million for the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and $1 million for the National Institute of Justice (NIJ) to conduct public health research into firearm morbidity and mortality prevention. Primary Care and the Physician Workforce: ACP urged Congress to support the Resident Physician Shortage Reduction Act of 2025 (S. 2439/ H.R. 4731), which would increase the number of Medicare supported direct graduate medical education (DGME) and indirect medical education (IME) positions by 14,000 over seven years. ACP supported the Conrad State 30 and Physician Access Reauthorization Act, S. 709 and H.R. 1585, to allow states to sponsor foreign-trained physicians to work in medically underserved areas in exchange for a waiver of the physicians' two-year foreign residence requirement. We supported the Resident Education Deferred Interest (REDI) Act (S 942/HR 2028) that, if passed, will allow borrowers to qualify for interest-free deferment on their student loans while serving in a medical or dental internship or residency program. ACP supported legislation for the H-1Bs for Physicians and Healthcare Workforce Act, H.R. 7961. The bill's primary goal is to exempt healthcare professionals from a $100,000 H-1B visa filing fee. ACP supported H.R. 8765, the Prioritizing Primary Care Act. This legislation would mandate an annual report on federal spending on primary care as well as establish a working group to study and make recommendations on how each federal agency addresses the issue. Scope of Practice: ACP provided comments urging the House Ways and Means Committee during markup to oppose the Equitable Community Access to Pharmacist Services Act, which would expand Medicare coverage to permanently include select services provided by a pharmacist. ACP advocated before Senate offices against the marked-up bill coming out of House Ways and Means and renamed the Main Street Pharmacy Access Act enabling pharmacists to bill certain Medicare codes and to diagnose and treat flu, strep throat and other respiratory infections. Expand Patient Access: We urged Congress to reintroduce and pass the Chronic Care Management Improvement Act. This legislation would have removed the cost sharing requirement for patients to access chronic care management services. We also support allowing the physician that performs chronic care management services to waive the requirement that the patient pay the 20 percent coinsurance fee associated with this service. We urged Congress to protect the public health infrastructure, recognize evidence-based science and preserve healthcare agency staffing to inform and protect the public from infectious disease and other health emergencies. Incidences of previously well-controlled, vaccine-preventable diseases, such as pertussis (whooping cough) and measles, are increasing in the United States. Vaccines are vital to our ability to prevent diseases that threaten public health, including novel diseases and future pandemics. We urged Congress to utilize the best possible scientific evidence to guide public health legislation. It is critical that public health leaders support evidence-based medicine, including the use of vaccines and other effective public health strategies that protect the public. ACP conducted a Hill Briefing on using scientifically driven, evidenced-based vaccines. Clinical Labs: Supported the provision in H.R. 6366 that would delay payment reductions and data reporting periods for the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule under the Protecting Access to Medicare Act (PAMA). Legislation could improve patient access to laboratory tests used to diagnose, monitor, prevent, and manage diseases for Medicare beneficiaries. Prescription Drug Reform: Supported the Capping Prescription Costs Act, introduced by Senator Raphael Warnock. The legislation would lower prescription drug costs for millions of Americans by placing annual caps on out-of-pocket costs for prescription drugs at $2,000 for individuals and $4,000 for families with private insurance. Supported bipartisan Drug-price Transparency for Consumers (DTC) Act, a bill that would require price disclosures on advertisements for prescription drugs in order to empower patients and reduce Americans colossal spending on medications. The bill was introduced by Senators Dick Durbin and Chuck Grassley. ACP also supported the Saving Seniors Money on Prescriptions Act, H.R. 950, which aims to drive down the rising costs of prescription drugs for patients on Medicare by improving price transparency in Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) business practices. Urged Congress to reintroduce and pass: 1) the Lowering Drug Costs for American Families Act, to expand the number of prescription drugs which Medicare can negotiate under the Inflation Reduction Act from 20 to 50 starting in 2029; 2) the Medicare PBM Accountability Act, legislation aimed at lowering the costs of prescription drugs for seniors covered by Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage plans; 3) the Increasing Access to Biosimilars Act of 2023, legislation which would encourage adoption of biosimilars in Medicare and improve biosimilar accessibility, by establishing a new pilot program - a voluntary, shared savings demonstration program - for providers of biosimilars in Medicare Part B; 4) the Cutting Copays Act, legislation which would eliminate cost-sharing for generic drugs for LIS beneficiaries, helping to incentivize the use of generic drugs; and the Drug Shortage Prevention Act of 2023, which would require that manufacturers of over-the-counter and prescription drugs notify Food & Drug Administration when they are unlikely to meet demand. ACP supported legislation, Drug-Price Transparency for Consumers (DTC) Act, by Senators. Durbin and Grassley that requires Direct-to-Consumer advertisements for prescription drugs and biological products paid for by Medicare and Medicaid to include the list price or Wholesale Acquisition Cost (WAC) for a 30-month supply-which is the price set by manufacturers (and which is paid by uninsured patients, as well as the 50 percent of patients with high-deductible plans).

lobbying_activities.description: NFDA works with relevant federal departments/agencies and Congress to support legislation, rules and regulations that improve funeral and burial benefits for Veterans and their families. Including supporting Take Care of America's Veterans Act ( H.R. 9237); Veteran Burial Timeliness and Death Certificate Accountability Act (H.R. 4398/S. 2309); Ensuring Veterans Final Resting Place Act (H.R. 647); Legislation to Increase Service-Connected Burial Benefits (S. 4108); Dennis and Lois Krisfalusy Act (H.R. 1344 / S.1127); (H.R. 9006) the Locating Our Unclaimed Veterans Act - improves identification of unclaimed veterans and helps locate next of kin; (H.R. 6921) the Hawaii National Cemetery Act - expands long-term access to national cemetery burial options for veterans and eligible family members in Hawaii; (H.R. 9321) the Unclaimed Veterans' Legacy Grant Program Act - assists organizations that conduct the research, outreach, and coordination necessary to honor unclaimed veterans.

NFDA works with relevant federal departments/agencies and Congress to support and/or advocate for legislation, rules and regulations that ensure the consensual donation and respectful disposition of human bodies and non-transplantable human body parts donated for education, research, and the advancement of medical, dental and mortuary science for research purposes. Including support The Consensual Donation and Research Integrity Act (S. 1270/H.R. 2589), which aims to bring federal oversight to the currently unregulated industry of whole-body donation.

NFDA works with relevant federal departments/agencies and Congress to ensure that the role of funeral service in any mass fatality disaster is clearly defined and adequately reflected in their policies.

Small Business: Health Care, Taxes and Related Issues NFDA works with relevant federal departments/agencies and Congress to support and/or advocate for legislation, rules and regulations that recognize the unique needs of small and family-owned businesses. Specifically, issues related to small business and tax related issues including Death Tax Repeal Act and including final expenses as a qualified expense in health savings accounts. Including support of Funeral Coverage Act (H.R. 2436); and Death Tax Repeal Act of 2025 (S. 587/H.R. 1301)

NFDA works with relevant federal departments/agencies and Congress to support and/or advocate for legislation, rules and regulations that address environmental health and safety issues related to funeral directors and the operation of funeral homes and crematories. Specifically, EPA and OSHA issues affecting funeral service, including issues related to formaldehyde exposure and use in embalming and the EPA TSCA Risk Evaluation. Including support of No IRIS Act of 2025 (S. 623/H.R. 1415):

H.R. 3514/S. 1816: Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act of 2025 - requires Medicare Advantage plans to implement electronic prior authorization, increase transparency, protect enrollees, and adhere to new response timeframes to improve timely access to care. H.R. 2433: Reducing Medically Unnecessary Delays in Care Act - mandates that prior authorization decisions under Medicare be made by qualified physicians, based on medical necessity and evidence-based standards, with transparency and input from practicing physicians. H.R. 9693, Patients First Act of 2026 would finally make structural changes needed to prevent cuts and create a payment system that helps ensure physicians can keep their doors open and provide seniors with quality, value-based healthcare. S. 1640/H.R. 879: Medicare Patient Access and Practice Stabilization Act of 2025 - This bill increases certain payment adjustments under the Medicare physician fee schedule for services furnished between April 1, 2025, and January 1, 2026. H.R. 8163/S. 5180: Provider Reimbursement Stability Act, to amend title XVIII of the Social Security Act to ensure stability for provider payments under the Medicare program. H.R. 8622: Medicare Physician Data-driven Performance Payment System Act to amend title XVIII of the Social Security Act to transform the Merit-based Incentive Payment System into the Data-driven Performance Payment System under the Medicare physician fee schedule H.R. 6160: Strengthening Medicare for Patients and Providers Act to modify certain adjustments to payment amounts under the Medicare physician fee schedule S. 1460/H.R. 786: Preserving Patient Access to Accountable Care Act - extends Medicare incentive payments for alternative payment models to 2027, with a new rate of 3.53 percent, to promote continued participation and improve healthcare efficiency. H.R. 2120/S. 1031: ROCR Value Based Program Act - establishes a new payment program for radiation oncology services, focusing on stable payments, quality care, and patient access, while exempting it from budget neutrality adjustments. H.R. 4559: Prompt and Fair Pay Act - to establish payment parity between Medicare Advantage and fee-for-service Medicare, and to establish prompt payment requirements under Medicare Advantage. H.R. 2484: Seniors' Access to Critical Medications Act of 2025 - establishes an exception to the physician self-referral prohibition for certain outpatient drugs under Medicare, mandates a study on drug dispensing practices, and reduces the Medicare improvement fund by $18 million. H.R. 4299: Protecting Patient Access to Cancer and Complex Therapies Act - provide for a rebate by manufacturers for selected drugs and biological products subject to maximum fair price negotiation. H.R. 4206/S. 1261: CONNECT for Health Act - expands access to telehealth services under Medicare H.R. 5081/S. 2709: Telehealth Modernization Act - to extend certain telehealth flexibilities under the Medicare program. H.R. 4752/S. 2760: Reducing Hereditary Cancer Act - to provide hereditary cancer genetic testing for individuals with a history of a hereditary cancer gene mutation. H.R. 8500: Timely Access to Coverage Decisions Act of 2026: To amend title XVIII of the Social Security Act to ensure timely review of local coverage determination requests under the Medicare program. H.R. 4331, Access to Claims Data Act: To require the Secretary of Health and Human Services to establish a process to expand access to claims data under certain Federal health plans in order to facilitate research and quality improvement.

H.R. 6423/S. 864: HELP Copays Act - requires health insurers to count third-party financial assistance toward patients' cost-sharing obligations, including deductibles and copays, for prescription drugs, with changes effective for plan years beginning January 1, 2026. S. 526: PBM Transparency Act - prevents unfair and deceptive acts or practices and the dissemination of false information related to pharmacy benefit management services for prescription drugs H.R. 4191/S. 1784: MAPS Act - requires federal agencies to regularly update a list of essential medicines, assess and report on supply chain risks, map pharmaceutical supply chains, and enhance coordination and cybersecurity to protect public health and national security. H.R. 3955/S.2062: RAPID Reserve Act - establishes a $500 million program to create and maintain domestic reserves of critical drugs and their ingredients, prioritizing domestic manufacturing and supply chain resilience to prevent shortages during public health emergencies. H.R. 8339: Drug Origin Transparency Act to amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to enhance drug manufacturing amount information reporting H.R. 5526/S. 1954: Biosimilar Red Tape Elimination Act - streamlines the approval process for biosimilar biological products by automatically deeming them interchangeable with reference products, subject to certain exclusivity protections, and requires updated regulatory guidance to reflect these changes. H.R. 4101: Cancer Drug Parity Act of 2025 - requires group health plans to provide cost-sharing for oral anticancer drugs that is at least as favorable as for provider-administered anticancer medications, with protections against increased patient costs and a mandated GAO study on the law's impact. H.R. 3521/S. 4440: Clinical Trials Modernization Act - Increase clinical trial participation among underrepresented populations by providing grants, permitting certain participant reimbursements, and offering tax exclusions, while ensuring compliance with existing legal protections. S. 705: Innovation in Pediatric Drugs Act of 2025 - amends existing laws to enhance pediatric cancer research, mandates compliance measures, allocates funding for pediatric studies, and sets guidelines for orphan drugs, with specific timelines for implementation and evaluation. H.R. 5509/S. 2903: Safe Step Act - to require a group health plan or health insurance coverage offered in connection with such a plan to provide an exceptions process for any medication step therapy protocol, and for other purposes. H.R. 4425/S. 2287: Palliative Care and Hospice Education and Training Act - expands federal support for workforce development, education, public awareness, and research in palliative and hospice care, with targeted funding and statutory changes to improve care for patients with serious or life-threatening illnesses. government_entities.name: Centers For Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)

lobbying_activities.description: (H.R. 529) - The Protecting Sensitive Locations Act - Expressed support for the Protecting Sensitive Locations Act. This legislation would codify the previous and longstanding guidance into law, prohibiting immigration enforcement actions by officers or agents at or within 1,000 feet of healthcare facilities such as hospitals, community health centers, and accredited health clinics. The protections in the bill also would extend to educational and social service facilities as well as places of worship, among others.

Urged Congress to increase funding for the Childrens Hospitals Graduate Medical Education (CHGME) program to $1.02 billion in FY 2027 to help address the growing pediatric workforce shortage. CHGME plays a critical role in training more than half of the nations pediatricians and specialists, ensuring children across the country have access to timely, high-quality care. Strengthening this program is essential to sustaining and expanding the pediatric care pipeline now and into the future. Urged Congress to increase FY 2027 funding for federal firearm injury prevention research, requesting $35 million for the CDC, $25 million for the NIH, and $1 million for the National Institute of Justice. This funding is critical to advancing evidence-based solutions to reduce firearm-related injuries, deaths, and suicides, and to strengthen public health and community safety nationwide. Expressed support for several provisions of the appropriations bill that extend expiring health programs and allocate funding for the Department of Labor, Health and Human Services, Education, and Related Agencies (Labor-HHS-ED). Urged Congress to find a solution that extends the Marketplace enhanced premium tax credits (EPTCs).

(H.R. 9504)- Tax Exempt Hospital Transparency Act- Expressed that Congress should first review existing oversight findings and determine whether additional requirements are necessary, targeted, and workable. (S. 3702/H.R. 7165) The Credit for Caring Act - Expressed support for the Credit Caring Act. The legislation would create a new, non-refundable federal tax credit for eligible working family caregivers to help address the financial challenges of caregiving.

Expressed support for Section 340B of the Public Health Service Act. Urged Congress to revise Section 2 in line with concerns expressed over discussion draft on rebate conditions; that the current HRSA standard of additional definitions in Section 4 remain in place; that Section 8 recognize that child sites operated through other appropriate affiliated structures, in addition to wholly owned facilities, align compliance requirements with existing Medicare provider-based standards, and reconsider the proposed charity-care and Medicaid/CHIP revenue benchmarks to account for state and community variation. (H.R. 9393) - The Lower Costs, More Transparency Act of 2026 and (H.R. 9390) - The Prices on the Wall Act of 2026 - Urged Congress to ensure that any new transparency requirements are aligned with existing federal rules, avoid duplication, recognize the complexity of health care pricing, and provide sufficient flexibility for hospitals serving diverse communities and patient populations. (H.R. 9645) - The Health Care Price Certainty for All Americans Act - Urged Congress to ensure that any new transparency requirements are aligned with existing federal rules, avoid duplication, recognize the complexity of health care pricing, and provide sufficient flexibility for hospitals serving diverse communities and patient populations. (S.2372/H.R.4581) - 340B PATIENTS Act of 2025-Expressed support for the 340B Patients Act. This legislation would codify 340B providers' ability to use contract pharmacies to dispense 340B discounted drugs, ensure that 340B patients can pick up their prescriptions at any local pharmacy, and allow safety-net providers to continue providing expanded medical and social services to their communities using their 340B discount savings. (S. 2287/H.R. 4425) - Palliative Care and Hospice Education and Training Act (PCHETA) - Expressed support for the Palliative Care and Hospice Education and Training Act (PCHETA). This legislation would increase the number of permanent faculty in palliative care in medical schools, nursing schools, and other programs, promote education and research in palliative care and hospice, and support the development of faculty careers in academic palliative and hospice (S. 380) - Rural Obstetrics Readiness Act - Expressed support for the Rural Obstetrics Readiness Act. This bipartisan legislation would ensure that rural health care facilities are equipped with targeted resources to provide high-quality obstetric care to women within their own communities.

Ensuring Patient Access to Critical Breakthrough Products Act of 2025(H.R. 5343 and S.1717) - Legislation to create automatic CMS coverage for devices approved via FDA's breakthrough pathway. (CMS rulemaking for Transitional Coverage of Emerging Technologies (TCET) - advocacy for a new, voluntary Transitional Coverage of Emerging Technologies (TCET) pathway that provides national Medicare coverage for Breakthrough-designated technologies, beginning on the date of FDA market authorization.) The Patient Access to Innovative New Technologies Act (PAINT Act) -- proposed legislation that aims to expand access to new medical technologies by improving the Medicare New Technology Add-on Payment (NTAP) program. It would create a single deadline for products in an alternative pathway, ensure breakthrough devices are eligible for conditional approval under NTAP, and prevent disruption in Medicare beneficiaries' access to new treatments. The Advancing Research for Chronic Pain Act (S. 5041), directs the CDC to regularly collect, analyze, and report data on the prevalence, burden, and impact of chronic pain in the US and build a centralized Chronic Pain Information Hub. The Relief of Chronic Pain Act (S. 3064), which would lower cost-sharing and bar step therapy and prior authorization for non-opioid treatments under Medicare Part D. Starting work on the Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act of 2026 (Public Law 117-328) - advocacy efforts on Medical Device User Fee Amendments (MDUFA) reauthorization, riders, and device shortages. Reauthorization of the Pandemic and All-Hazards Preparedness Act (PAHPA) (Public Law 109-417) - advocacy on risk mitigation plans and voluntary shortage reporting related to medical device supply chains and advocacy for medical research and to foster a new era of medical innovation and prepare for future pandemics and promote health equity. Support passage of the Radiation Oncology Case Rate (ROCR) Value Based Payment Program Act of 2025 - Senate (S. 1031) & (H.R. 2120). This legislation would increase access to patient care, enhance the quality of cancer treatments, encourage innovation, reduce disparities for rural and underserved patients, and lower patient costs by saving Medicare about $200 million over 10 years. The WISeR Model (Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction Model) - Advocacy efforts on inclusions in CMS' WISeR model, which is aimed at reducing inappropriate care and preventing improper payments under Medicare Part B by refining prior authorization processes for traditional fee-for-service Medicare. Engaged on the Regulatory Alignment for Predictable and Immediate Device (RAPID) coverage pathway and efforts to streamline FDA-CMS coordination and Medicare coverage for Breakthrough Devices.

lobbying_activities.description: During this lobbying period I largely contacted Alaska's congressional delegation via e-mail to convey Alaska Power Association's support for certain issues. Those issues were: Urging support for a letter asking Secretary Burgum to use existing authorities under Section 512 of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA) to improve utilities ability to reduce wildfire risk in and around their rights-of-way across public lands and forests Urging via letter that U.S. Treasury Deputy Assistant Secretary Don Snyder release of the Hydropower Safe Harbor Table as soon as practicable. Sharing APA's comments on a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking implementing Section 2209 of the FAA Extension, Safety, and Security Act of 2016, which establishes a process for certain critical infrastructure owners and operators to apply for Unmanned Aircraft Flight Restrictions ("UAFRs"). In short, the rule would allow eligible facilities to request FAA approval to prohibit or limit drone operations in the immediate vicinity of qualifying infrastructure. APA filed comments asking the FAA to revise its proposed drone-restriction rule so that eligibility is based on a facilitys operational importance, lack of redundancy, restoration challenges, and national security role, rather than primarily on size or customer counts, and if the FAA will not do that nationally, to create Alaska-specific criteria and lower eligibility thresholds for Alaskas critical infrastructure. APA also held a meeting in August with FERC Commissioner Lindsay See and Sen. Lisa Murkowski at our office to discuss various issues relating to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

During this period I participated in two federal fly-in conferences. One conference was with the Northwest Public Power Association in which I participated as a representative of Alaska. We met with congressional offices from Alaska and Washington. We advocated for: H.R. 471/S.1462, the Fix our Forest Act; H.R 2492/s.349, the Fire Safe Electrical Corridors Act; supported the forestry title provisions in the Farm Bill (H.R. 7576); H.R. 4669 the FEMA Reform Act; H.R. 164 the POWER Act; H.R. 3657 the Hydropower Relicensing Transparency Act; S.3518, the FLOWS Act. We also supported fully funding the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) and the SPEED Act, H.R. 4776. All of these issues would be advantageous to Alaska's electric utilities. I organized and conducted the Alaska Power Association federal fly-in, which brought 16 of our electric utility members to D.C. We met with our congressional delegation and advocated for the same issues listed above. We also updated our congressional members on current events with Alaska's electric utilities. We also met with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to advocate for more streamlined hydropower licensing and relicensing, along with other issues; the DOE Office of Energy Dominance Financing to explore how that office might assist with Alaska electric utility projects; Rural Utilities Service Assistance Administrator Christopher McLean to learn more about the available RUS programs. During this reporting period I also advocated for full funding of the LIHEAP program with Alaska's congressional delegation via e-mail, and worked with Sen. Murkowski's office on some language for her FLOWS Act legislation.

lobbying_activities.description: END ICE KILLINGS: This message to Congress, a sign-on from faith organizations including NAC, expresses outrage regarding July 2026 ICE killings in Texas and Maine. In Houston, ICE shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a beloved resident and father who was on his way to work on July 7 in the citys East End. On July 13 in Biddeford, Maine, ICE also shot and killed Johan Sebastian, a 25-year-old husband and father of a three-year-old daughter. The letter addresses the need for training standards as well as reallocation of budget funds. The letter ends with "as people of faith, we believe public funding should go toward caring for our communities, rather than fueling agencies that are killing our neighbors and tearing families apart." DREAM AND PROMISE ACT DISCHARGE PETITION (H.R. 1589): NAC was part of this sign-on to members of the House of Representatives re: protections for immigrant youth, Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) recipients, and Temporary Protective Status (TPS) holders. These protections are long overdue and the urgent need for permanent protections is more pressing than ever. With the June 2026 devastating TPS ruling by the Supreme Court and the continuous DACA renewal delays, detentions, and even deportations - our communities cannot wait a moment longer. Congress must act now. The letter calls for a discharge petition: if 218 Members of the House of Representatives agree and sign on, the bill will be moved out of committee and brought to the floor for a vote. TEMPORARY PROTECTED STATUS REDESIGNATION FOR VENEZUELA: Letter to President Trump, Secretary Mullin, Dept. of Homeland Security, Secretary Rubio, Dept. of State. NAC is part of an organizational letter urging Secretary Mullin of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to re-designate Venezuela for Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for an 18-month designation, as recent events merit reconsideration of country conditions. Reports have shown that there have been no significant changes over the years concerning the human rights situation. Even after U.S. intervention, which ousted Nicolas Maduro from power, Venezuela continues to remain under authoritarianism. In addition, the recent devastating 7.2 and 7.5 magnitude earthquakes that struck the country on June 24 caused a major humanitarian impact and showed the governments lack of coordination, emergency response, and relief efforts. As of July 12, 2026, the USGS reported more than 4,400 persons killed, approximately 16,600 injured, and nearly 30,000 missing. According to the United Nations Development Program (UNDP), the earthquakes caused an estimated $6.7 billion in immediate physical damage. TEMPORARY PROTECTIVE STATUS (TPS) FOR EL SALVADOR: NAC was part of this sign-on urging the Department of Homeland Security Secretary to extend the TPS designation for El Salvador before it is scheduled to expire on Sept. 9, 2026. Current conditions in El Salvador do not support a safe return for holders living in the U.S. MEDICARE IMMIGRANT ELIGIBILITY CHANGES: NAC joined the Justice in Aging sign-on letter commenting on the proposed rules implementing H.R. 1 restrictions on Medicare eligibility. The letter outlines key issues and the impact the rule will have on older immigrants, including those who are dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid. The letter urges the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to adopt a person-centered equitable approach to the implementation of Medicare eligibility changes presented in the CY 2027 Medicare Physician fee Schedule. Letter directed to Dr. Mehmet Oz, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, U.S. Dept of Health and Human Services. ENDORSEMENT OF TEMPORARY PROTECTIVE STATUS (TPS) FOR NEPAL: Letter to President Trump and Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Department of Homeland Security urging TPS for Nepal. Triggered by a massive collapse of glacier ice and rock high in the Himalayas near the Nepal-China border, flooding sent a destructive surge of water, sediment, rock, and debris through downstream communities in Nepal, causing extensive loss of life and widespread destruction. Communities have been displaced, homes and livelihoods have been lost, and critical infrastructure-including roads, bridges, schools, health facilities, and power systems-has been damaged or destroyed. Nepal now faces the immediate work of supporting affected communities and restoring essential services while beginning a substantial reconstruction effort. The letter endorses Congressional leaders call for TPS designation for Nepal. REFUGEE GREEN CARD PROCESSING, RE-VETTING, AND MEDICAID CUTS: NAC joined this letter opposing the ongoing green card processing freeze and refugee "re-vetting" efforts. The letter focuses on the interaction between the green card adjudication halt and the coming Medicaid and CHIP eligibility changes that cut off refugees who do not have green cards (including over 149,000 with pending applications). The letter urges DHS and USCIS to immediately resume adjudication of all refugee green card applications, end unnecessary re-vetting of resettled refugees, and establish a channel for members of Congress to request expedited adjudication for applicants facing a loss of medical coverage. PROTECT A FAIR, COMPLETE AND ACCURATE 2030 CENSUS: The U.S. Census Bureau published a proposed regulation that would make significant changes to how the 2030 Decennial Census counts people and collects demographic data. If implemented, the proposed changes would directly impact the people and communities that nonprofits serve every day and undermine the census's ability to provide a fair and accurate count of the people living in America. The proposal would exclude broad categories of people, including international students, H-1B visa holders, refugees, asylum seekers, undocumented people and others, from the population count used to allocate congressional seats and federal funding. The proposed regulation would also eliminate questions on race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation, an unprecedented departure from the censuss longstanding practice of collecting critical demographic information. These changes would undercount the number of people living in communities, reducing their access to federal resources and political representation, and they would make it harder to understand changing community needs and address racial, social, and other disparities. ICE SENSITIVE LOCATIONS POLICY IN PLACES OF WORSHIP: Upon request of Muslim Advocates.org, and the National Immigration Law Center, NAC, along with other faith-based organizations were invited to sign on to an amicus brief that discusses the harm of immigration enforcement in places of worship with a focus on anti-Muslim targeting. The brief also situates these harms within the broader pattern of racialized and anti-Muslim national security policies that have historically targeted specific communities and have implications for all immigrant communities. NAC QUOTE IN INTERFAITH IMMIGRATION COALITION PRESS RELEASE ON TEMPORARY PROTECTIVE STATUIS TERMINATION: Fran Eskin-Royer, Executive Director of the National Advocacy Center of the Sisters of the Good Shepherd, said: America opened our arms, recognizing the severity of life in unsafe societies such as Haiti and El Salvador. Life has not improved in these countries. Rather, men, women and children are barely surviving in places like Haiti, overcome with violence and poverty. Now is not the time to end Temporary Protected Status, forcing these innocent individuals and families back to countries in turmoil and crisis. We call on the Trump Administration and U.S. Congress to extend TPS, and, in particular for Haiti, to pass S. 4814 extending TPS for Haitians for three years. STATEMENT FOR UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY HIGH-LEVEL WEEK AND 75TH ANNIVERSARY YEAR OF THE REFUGEE CONVENTION: NAC joined faith-based organizations in expressing deep concern for ongoing human rights violations experienced by refugees, asylum seekers , and other forcibly displaced people as part of acknowledging the 75th anniversary year. The statement urges all member states to reaffirm their commitment to the Refugee convention and other international human rights instruments, ensuring that dignity, solidarity, protection, and responsibility-sharing remain at the center of responses to forced displacement, upholding the rights of refugees towards a more just, peaceful, and humane world. NAC QUOTE IN INTERFAITH IMMIGRATION COALITION PRESS RELEASE ON PRESIDENTIAL DETERMINATION NUMBER: Fran Eskin-Royer, Executive Director of the National Advocacy Center of the Sisters of the Good Shepherd: Displacement and fear do not take a holiday; nor do they take a pause for U.S. midterm elections. Americans would be mortified to discover that our great country has only welcomed around 15,000 vetted refugees in the last year - and that over 95% of them are white Afrikaners leaving South Africa. Meanwhile, there are more than 41 million refugees from the rest of the world who purposefully are being prohibited entry or even consideration. What of those escaping Myanmar and Ukraine? What of all the Christians being persecuted and hunted in Nigeria and Sudan? The Trump Administration must fully resume the governments refugee processing and resettlement program, including a nondiscriminatory framework to protect the most at-risk refugees. And, for the love of God, the miserably low cap must be raised dramatically. IMMIGRATION ADVOCACY VISITS (Sept 15): Our Lady of Sorrows Mass, Procession and Advocacy - Advocated for Immigration Principles paralleling the 7 sorrowful mysteries of the rosary. Organized by the Dorothea Project - a group of Catholic women from around the U.S. organized for action around Catholic Social Teaching for the dignity and rights of immigrants and all vulnerable people. . NAC met with Rep. Conaway, (NJ-3) staff, Sen. Booker staff and Rep. Crockett (TX-30) staff.

PROTECT MEDICAID FROM FURTHER RECONCILIATION CUTS: NAC was part of a letter urging members of Congress to oppose any further cuts or harmful changes to Medicaid through any budget reconciliation or other legislation. PROTECT BABIES AND FAMILIES IN FY2027 APPROPRIATIONS: NAC was among the signers of this letter to members of the House and Senate Appropriations Committees calling for policy decisions to be grounded in principles that support babies, toddlers, and their families. This letter highlights many programs that could be harmed and must be protected including Head Start and Early Head Start, Child Care and Development Block Grants, and Individuals with Disabilities Education Act programs. NATIONAL DEFENSE AUTHORIZATION ACT (NDAA) FISCAL YEAR 2027 (HR 8800): Request for NAC advocates to urge their representatives to vote NO on the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 2027 (HR 8800), unless the SAVE America Act (S 1383), as passed by the House, is removed. HEALTHY START PROGRAM (MATERNAL HEALTH): NAC was part of this sign on from state and national organizations urging Congress to fully fund Healthy Start for FY2027 (from October 1, 2026, through September 30, 2027). Like previous sign-on letters, this letter was meant to demonstrate the depth of support for Healthy Start across the nation. THE CENSUS PROJECT BUDGET: White House released its initial list of Fiscal Year 2027 funding anomalies. To reflect this unexpected development, the sign-on organizers made some minor edits to a previous Census-related sign-on to Congress; specifically: If the current appropriations process lapses, we urge you to reinforce your commitment to the U.S. Census Bureau by adding the agency to the Administrations requested list of funding anomalies as deliberations regarding the FY 2027 Commerce, Justice, Science Appropriations bill continue. NAC was among the signers. PROTECT NUTRITION FOR WOMEN, INFANTS AND CHILDREN (WIC) THROUGH REMOTE SERVICES LEGISLATIONT: NAC constituents are urging their members of Congress to pass the MODERN WIC Act/21st Century WIC Act (H.R.1464/S. 3842) by including them in the FY 2027 Agriculture Appropriations. These bipartisan, bicameral bills would make permanent the virtual (such as video or telephone) certification/recertification, benefit distribution, nutrition education and breastfeeding support options for the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants and Children (WIC) which are set to expire as early as October 1, 2026. (Until recent years, families were required to have in-person appointments to get certified for, pick up, and reload WIC benefits.) MODERN WIC ACT / 21st Century WIC ACT: (H.R.1464/S. 3842) ACTION ALERT: NAC constituents were asked to advocate for future students and moms by contacting their members of Congress to pass these acts by including them in the FY2027 Agricultural Appropriations. JOINT STATEMENT WITH OTHER CONGREGATIONS ON U.S. COVENANT FOR OUR FUTURE (EFFORT TO REPEAL H.R. 1): Covenant For Our Future is a rising multi faith, multi issue movement mobilizing thousands of leaders across traditions and communities to repeal H.R. 1 (the One Big Beautiful Bill Act) and renew the federal governments commitment to justice. NAC is among those that affirmed / signed the Covenant. Our country is facing a convergence of crises-escalating threats to democracy, cuts to healthcare and the social safety net, racist persecution of migrants, fast growing climate impacts, and massive tax breaks for the wealthiest that violate our deepest moral commitments. $1.15 TRILLION PENTAGON BUDGET: NAC was a part of this sign-on letter focused on opposing the $1.15 trillion Pentagon budget. The letter had three main asks: 1.Reject the $1.15 trillion Pentagon topline and oppose any further increase in Pentagon funding for FY 2027, including plus-ups sought through supplemental or reconciliation packages. 2.Protect and invest in programs that make life more affordable for those struggling. Ensure adequate investment in human needs programs, including Medicare, the Affordable Care Act and SNAP, and ensure Pentagon spending does not further eclipse non-defense spending. 3.Refuse to fund unauthorized war, including Iran, Latin America and elsewhere, and invest instead in the true sources of security-diplomacy, peacebuilding, foreign assistance, and nonviolent approaches to human, national, and global security.

ADVOCACY FOR CUBA: The Trump administration's policies have pushed Cuba into a full-blown humanitarian crisis, and the signs now point to a possible military escalation. U.S. military planners are reportedly already examining options for action on the island, including an air assault involving thousands of soldiers. The public groundwork is being laid as well: last week, the State Department released a 100-page report casting Cuba as the driving force behind "far left terrorism" in the United States. Many observers, including members of Congress, have read it as an effort to manufacture consent for military intervention. NAC and collaborators asked the Senate to address this issue before they recess for summer break. JULY 14 HUMAN TRAFFICKING BRIEFING AND ADVOCACY: NAC helped organize and promote a July 14 briefing for House and Senate staff around two pieces of legislation, the Frederick Douglass TVPRA (H.R. 1144 - Foreign Relations focus) and the Kids Online Safety Act (S. 1748 - Science & Technology focus). The briefing was followed by in person lobby visits on July 14. NAC made visits on the two bills to Rep. Stephen Lynch MA-08, Rep. Gabe Evans CO-08, Rep. David Kustoff TN-08, and Senator Bill Hagerty TN. NAC advocates also did online email advocacy on the two bills on or around July 14. ACCOUNTABILITY FOR BOAT STRIKES ON ONE-YEAR ANNIVERSARY: The sign-on letter to Congress marked the one-year anniversary (September 2) since the first boat strike in Latin America and urged Congress to adopt an aggressive oversight and accountability agenda to redress these illegal and immoral operations. HOUSE VOTE ON THE CUBA WAR POWER RESOLUTION: NAC joined this letter urging House Democratic leadership to call a vote on a Cuba War Powers Resolution as soon as possible and oppose the White House's illegal oil blockade. Since January 2026, President Trump has declared a functional U.S. blockade on Cuban-bound oil, widely understood to be an illegal act of war under international law. Trump's oil embargo has pushed Cuba to the brink of humanitarian collapse, and a UN panel last week that U.S. sanctions threaten to make Cuba into a "silent Gaza". Trump and Secretary Rubio continue to announce new sanctions and interventions in Cuba aimed at fomenting regime change, as well as threaten direct military intervention on the island. ACT TO STOP U.S. GUN TRAFFICKING - ARMAS ACT Action Alert: Constituents of NAC were asked to write to Congress urging their members to co-sponsor the Americas Regional Monitoring of Arms Sales (ARMAS) Act of 2025 (H.R. 6736 / S.3508); this legislation would profoundly impact Latin America and the Caribbean, reducing gun violence, promoting regional stability, and preventing U.S. firearms from contributing to humanitarian crises there. It would effectively stop the illegal flow of U.S. weapons and ammunition to Latin America and the Caribbean. ARMAS Act (Sept 29/30): Coalition of 20+ organizations (incl NAC) advocating for the Americas Regional Monitoring of Arms Sales (ARMAS) Act of 2025 (H.R. 6736 / S.3508); this legislation would profoundly impact Latin America and the Caribbean - particularly Mexico and Haiti, reducing gun violence, promoting regional stability, and preventing U.S. firearms from contributing to humanitarian crises there. Sept 29 included a briefing on the Hill featuring people impacted by gun violence in Haiti and Mexico, and other experts on the regions and legislation. After the briefing advocates took part in a training and heard from additional experts on Haiti and Mexico. Sept 30 was devoted to online and in person advocacy.

SNAP (SUPPLEMENTAL NUTRITION ASSISTANCE PROGRAM): Hunger is a daily experience for millions in the U.S. As living costs rise and wages lag, the One Big Beautiful Bill Acts (OBBBA) significant cuts to SNAP remain. NAC Constituents were asked to alert their members of Congress to reverse the SNAP cuts, undo the new state-level benefit cost-shifts and undo the additional 25% administrative fee by passing a Farm Bill that rectifies these program harms. The Congressional Budget Office estimates that states will be forced to contribute $35 billion to meet these changes or forego the program entirely. VOTE NO ON FARM BILL: NAC blasted the members of the Senate Agricultural Committee urging them to vote NO on the revised Farm Bill recently released by the Senate Agriculture Committee Chairman Boozman. The bill would delay the SNAP benefit cost-share to the states for only ONE year and increase the costs states may have to pay for SNAP. The committee members were asked to continue to pursue a bipartisan solution that: gives states and communities more time to adapt to the changes to SNAP brought by H.R. 1; keeps food on families tables and invests wisely in children and farmers.

FAMILY STABILITY AND OPPORTUNITY VOUCHERS ACT (S. 5405): The Family Stability and Opportunity Vouchers Act was to be reintroduced in Sept. 2026 - and was, in fact, as S. 5405. The co-sponsors requested endorsing organizations and NAC obliged. The Act focuses on increasing housing options for low-income families experiencing or at risk of homelessness.

DOMESTIC VIOLENCE (DV) SURVIVORS ALERTED FOR EMERGENCY (SAFE) NOTICE ACT OF 2026 (S. 5656): NAC was among the organizations endorsing this bill that would require DV victims and survivors be notified when a prohibited abusive intimate partner fails a firearms background check. Shared with members of Congress.

AIDS RELIEF: NAC was part of this sign-on letter urging Congress to protect the Presidents Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) from a new State Department plan to shut off funding that is critical for the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) work on PEPFAR and Global Health Security. MEDICARE: NAC was part of a sign-on letter asking Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to prioritize pro-consumer reforms and to ensure health care consumers can access the affordable, high-quality hospital care they need and deserve. In July 2026, the Trump Administration proposed major changes to how Medicare pays for hospital care in its annual Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS). If finalized, these proposals would take important steps to rein in key payment distortions, including site of service payment differences, that drive hospital consolidation and unaffordable hospital care. PRESCRIPTION DRUG COSTS: NAC was part of this sign-on urging policymakers in the Senate to build on the Inflation Reduction Act with policies to save hundreds of billions of dollars in prescription drug costs and make sure all Americans have access to the medicines they need. Sent to Ranking Member Wyden of the Senate Finance Committee and other Senate Democrats in response to their request for information from stakeholders on policies to lower drug prices and make drugs more affordable for patients.

CHILD TAX CREDIT (CTC): This sign-on letter from NAC and others to congressional leadership expressed support for expansion of the Child Tax Credit (CTC). It endorsed the American Family Act (AFA) to expand the CTC by increasing the credit, making it fully available to all children on a monthly basis, and creating a baby bonus. The letter also urged congressional leaders to make the AFA a cornerstone of the federal affordability agenda. CHILD TAX CREDIT AND EARNED INCOME TAX CREDIT: NAC joined a coalition letter urging Congressional leaders to include direct cash policies in any affordability agenda. The request is to: 1. Expand the Child Tax Credit by making it fully available to low- and middle-income families, including all children regardless of immigration status, and delivering it in monthly payments. 2. Expand the Earned Income Tax Credit by broadening age and income eligibility and increasing the credit for workers without children. AFFORDABILITY AND THE CHILD TAX CREDIT: NAC signed on to two additional letters to Congress: 1.Cash & Affordability Letter The letter calls on Congress to make direct cash supports-including an expanded monthly Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit-part of any affordability agenda. The letter highlights policies that can help families and workers meet rising costs and calls for expanding the CTC and EITC to reach more people. 2.American Family Act (S. 1393 / H.R. 2763) Sign-On Letter This letter urges Congress to pass the American Family Act, which would expand the Child Tax Credit, make it fully available to children in low- and middle-income families, provide enhanced support for newborns, and deliver payments monthly. The letter highlights the role of an expanded CTC in helping families meet basic needs and addressing the rising cost of raising children.

OCCUPATION OF DC BY MIILITARY: August 11, 2026 marked one year of military occupation of DC. NAC was a part of this open letter to Congress marking the occasion and noting the deep harms inflicted over the past year. Topics include: 1) Oppose the military occupation and full support of DC statehood. 2) That every governor serving as Commander in Chief of deployed National Guard troops withdraw those troops from Washington, D.C. immediately. 3) Call on every Member of Congress to honor the principle of consent of the governed and commit to not overturning or interfering with Washington, D.C.'s locally enacted laws. Congress' constitutional jurisdiction over the federal enclave should not be used as an excuse to take away the authority DC has over its own affairs. 4) Urge the federal government to dismantle the "DC Safe and Beautiful Task Force" and the Joint Task Force created to operationalize it, to end the surge of forces in Washington, D.C., and to cease all ICE, DHS, DEA, IRS, FBI, Park Police, and other federal surge traffic checkpoints, high speed chases, and raids on homes and workplaces. 5) Encourage our communities to use their First Amendment rights in the District of Columbia to peaceably assemble and petition their government for a redress of grievances. 6) Publicly oppose any effort to prevent the seating of duly elected officials representing Washington, D.C. or any other jurisdiction and commit our resources to ensure that every elected official is sworn in and seated.

KIDS ONLINE SAFETY ACT (S.1748) Action Alert: NAC has advocated several years for the passage of this Act. Some progress has taken place. Meta was recently held accountable in court for its addictive design features. lobbying_activities.description: H.R. 9171, Department of the Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2027, Title II (Environmental Protection Agency), State and Tribal Assistance Grants account, provisions relating to Clean Water and Drinking Water State Revolving Fund capitalization grants, and the Senate FY2027 Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies appropriations process: Advocated for funding Clean Water State Revolving Fund (CWSRF) and Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF) capitalization grants at $6.5B each ($13B combined) in FY2027, including opposition to proposed reductions below FY2026 enacted levels and to Community Project Funding/Congressionally Directed Spending deductions from SRF capitalization grant accounts. Educated Members of Congress and staff, through meetings, written communications, and state-specific impact materials, on the projected decline in SRF capitalization funding to states resulting from the expiration of Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) supplemental SRF appropriations after FY2026. H.R. 6500, Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027 (P.L. 119-103), Division A, provisions governing FY2027 State Revolving Fund capitalization grant funding and the provision prohibiting the Office of Management and Budget from finalizing its proposed Uniform Guidance revisions before December 11, 2026: Advocated for maintaining Clean Water and Drinking Water State Revolving Fund capitalization grant funding under the FY2027 continuing resolution, and for delaying the Office of Management and Budgets proposed revisions to the Uniform Guidance (2 CFR Part 200) given their impact on the administration of State Revolving Fund programs.

H.R. 9497 and S. 4949, Water Resources Development Act of 2026, including S. 4949 Division B (Drinking Water and Wastewater Infrastructure): Advocated for reauthorization of the Clean Water State Revolving Fund (Clean Water Act Title VI) and Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (Safe Drinking Water Act Section 1452) at $6.5B annually for each program, including the SRF reauthorization provisions in Division B of S. 4949, and for inclusion of SRF reauthorization in the final WRDA 2026 legislation. S. 5016, Clean Water Allotment Modernization Act of 2026: Engaged on proposed changes to the Clean Water State Revolving Fund allotment formula and their effect on state SRF programs. S. 5368, Water Cyber Shield Act of 2026: Engaged on proposed authorization of additional Drinking Water and Clean Water State Revolving Fund funding for water system cybersecurity, and on administration of that funding through state SRF programs. S. 4812, FIRE SMART Act of 2026: Engaged on the proposed expansion of Drinking Water State Revolving Fund eligibility to include water infrastructure projects with wildfire suppression benefits, including concerns about expanding eligible uses without a corresponding increase in SRF funding.

Lobbied the House and Senate in support of the Prevent Government Shutdowns Act (H.R. 5870 / S. 4632) that would implement an automatic continuing resolution on rolling 14-day periods, based on the most current spending levels enacted in the previous fiscal year. Lobbied in support of S. 3012, the Shutdown Fairness Act, to ensure essential federal workers, active-duty military, and some contractors receive pay and benefits during a government shutdown, rather than waiting until it ends

Lobbied Congress in support of S. 2837, the Protect Americas Workforce Act to rescind EO to eliminate federal collective bargaining rights. Lobbied in opposition to augmentation and in support of full staffing, funding and workplace safety for correctional officers and all BOP staff. Lobbied in support of H.R. 378 and S. 83, the "Thin Blue Line Act," which would make murdering a law enforcement officer an aggravated factor in sentencing for a capital crime. Lobbied in support of H.R. 1556 and S. 718, "Eric's Law," which would allow the empaneling of a new jury if a jury fails to reach a unanimous verdict in a trial involving the murder of a law enforcement officer. Lobbied in support of S. 736, the Lieutenant Osvaldo Albarati Stopping Prison Contraband Act, introduced by Senator Jon Ossoff (D-GA) and Senator Chuck Grassley (R-IA) to crack down on the smuggling of contraband cellphones into federal prisons by upgrading the charge for such smuggling from a misdemeanor offense to a felony. Lobbied in opposition to removal of Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) Commissioners. Lobbied in support of full funding and staffing at EEOC. Lobbied against EEOC proposed rule on antidiscrimination. Lobbied against government shutdown and RIFs. Lobbied in support of H.R. 7137/S. 3068 the Shutdown Fairness Act.

Lobbied against H.R. 9237/S. 4744, the Take Care of Americas Veterans Act, Which further privatizes the VA, moves psychologist from hybrid to full title 38 and pays for new benefits for veterans by cutting other veteran benefits. Lobbied against a provision in S. 3466 Honor Our Promise to Veterans Act of 2025 that would move psychologist from hybrid to full title 38. Lobbied in support of H.R. 657, the "VA CPE Modernization Act." Lobbied the House and Senate in support of H.R. 7148, the Continuing Appropriations, Act, 2026 providing appropriations to several federal departments and agencies for the remainder of FY2026 and providing continuing FY2026 appropriations for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) through February 13, 2026. It also extends various expiring programs and authorities. Lobbied the House in support of H.R. 7147 as amended and passed by the Senate on March 27, the Homeland Security and Further Additional Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026. Lobbied in support of S. 3168 / H.R. 7137, the Shutdown Fairness Act, to ensure federal workers, active-duty military, and some contractors receive pay and benefits during a government shutdown, rather than waiting until it ends. Advised House and Senate members on FY27 appropriations with respect to the federal workforce as the FY27 appropriations process began.

Lobbied Congress in support of S. 2837, the Protect Americas Workforce Act to rescind EO to eliminate federal collective bargaining rights. Lobbied opposing cuts to pay and benefits in reconciliation instructions. Lobbied Congress to require Federal Bureau of Prisons to provide safe staffing and workplace safety measures for correctional officers. Lobbied in opposition to the closure of FCI Terminal Island in Los Angeles, CA. Lobbied in opposition to augmentation and in support of full staffing, funding and workplace safety for correctional officers and all BOP staff. Lobbied for higher funding levels for Bureau of Prisons (BOP) and continued prohibition of closure of minimum-security camps; lobbied for funding to: hire adequate numbers of correctional staff; end the use of augmentation to compensate for lack of hiring correctional officer positions; alleviate overcrowding at high-security institutions; to increase unit officer staff at high security institutions; and reduce the use of BOP contract prisons. Lobbied in support of H.R. 378 and S. 83, the "Thin Blue Line Act," which would make murdering a law enforcement officer an aggravated factor in sentencing for a capital crime. Lobbied in support of H.R. 1556 and S. 718, "Eric's Law," which would allow the empaneling of a new jury if a jury fails to reach a unanimous verdict in a trial involving the murder of a law enforcement officer. Lobbied in support of S. 736, the Lieutenant Osvaldo Albarati Stopping Prison Contraband Act, introduced by Senator Jon Ossoff (D-GA) and Senator Chuck Grassley (R-IA) to crack down on the smuggling of contraband cellphones into federal prisons by upgrading the charge for such smuggling from a misdemeanor offense to a felony. Lobbied in opposition to removal of Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) Commissioners. Lobbied in support of full funding and staffing at EEOC. Lobbied against government shutdown and RIFs. Lobbied in support of H.R. 7137/S. 3068 the Shutdown Fairness Act. Lobbied in support of DHS pay.

Lobbied Congress on the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027. Lobbied Congress in support of restoring collective bargaining rights for civilian employees of the U.S. Department of Defense. Lobbied Congress in support increasing wages for U.S. Department of Defense civilian employees. Lobbied Congress in support of the Arsenal Workload Sustainment Act, H.R. 1995/S. 905). Lobbied Congress in support of the Federal Firefighters Families First Act (H.R. 759). Lobbied in support of incentives and policies in support of domestic shipbuilding. Lobbied in support of the Department of Defenses right to repair military equipment by requiring DOD agencies to only enter procurement contractors if the contractor agrees to provide fair and reasonable access to repair materials. Lobbied opposing efforts to privatize Department of Defense commissary services. Lobbied opposing Reductions in Force (RIFs) to civilian Department of Defense employees.

Lobbied the House and Senate in support of H.R. 7148, the Continuing Appropriations, Act, 2026, providing appropriations to the District of Columbia and several federal departments and agencies for the remainder of FY2026 and providing continuing FY2026 appropriations for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) through February 13, 2026.

Lobbied Congress in support of S. 2837, the Protect Americas Workforce Act to rescind EO to eliminate federal collective bargaining rights. Lobbied opposing cuts to pay and benefits in reconciliation instructions. Lobbied against funding cuts of the meat and poultry inspection program. Lobbied against further expanding the program of putting plant employees, not inspectors, in charge of quality control and contamination. Lobbied against budget cuts to Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS) full-time staffing given current vacancies of Food Inspectors and Consumer Safety Inspectors. Lobbied against budget cuts that lead to staffing cuts at the Economic Research Service (ERS) and National Institute on Food and Agriculture (NIFA). Lobbied to prohibit funds from being spent to create a modernized beef slaughter inspection system or issue line speed waivers to beef, poultry, or hog slaughter plants. Lobbied against elimination, consolidation, reductions in force and budget cuts to the Beltsville Agricultural Research Service and FSIS positions across the country. Lobbied against government shutdown and RIFs. Lobbied in opposition to increased line speed proposed rule. Lobbied in support of H.R. 7137 / S. 3068, the Shutdown Fairness Act. Lobbied in support of DHS pay.

lobbying_activities.description: Older Americans Act Reauthorization. The Older Americans Act Reauthorization Act (S. 2120): Proposals to reauthorize the Older Americans Act (OAA) of 1965 and to increase the authorization of appropriations for OAA programs, which is the major federal discretionary funding source for home and community-based services for older adults and their caregivers. Programs supported through the OAA include home-delivered and congregate nutrition services, in-home supportive services, transportation, caregiver support, community service employment, health and wellness programs, the long-term care ombudsman program, services to prevent the abuse, neglect, and exploitation of older adults, and other supportive services. Social Security Cost of Living Adjustment (COLA). The Fair COLA for Seniors Act (No bill) and the Social Security Cost of Living Increase Act (No bill): Proposals to adopt the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E) for the purpose of determining COLAs for Social Security beneficiaries; the Boosting Benefits and COLAs for Seniors Act (S. 3059/H.R. 5841): Proposal to calculate COLAs using the current Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) or the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E), whichever is greater. Social Security Expansion. The Social Security 2100 Act (H.R. 9519/S. 5042): Proposals to improve benefits and to strengthen Social Security's financing by altering the payroll tax cap, among other changes. The Social Security Expansion Act (S. 770 and H.R. 1700): Proposals to enhance Social Security benefits and ensure the long-term solvency of the Social Security program. The Strengthening Social Security Act (H.R. 9296): Proposals to extend the solvency of the Social Security Trust Funds and improve benefits. The Safeguarding American Families & Expanding Social Security Act (S. 3462 and H.R. 9415): Proposals to update and modernize Social Security benefits and to extend solvency of the Social Security Trust Funds. The Protecting and Preserving Social Security Act (S. 2614 and H.R. 4968): Proposals to adopt the Consumer Price Index for the Elderly (CPI-E) for the purpose of determining COLAs for Social Security beneficiaries and to ensure the long-term solvency of the Social Security program by altering the payroll tax cap. The Protecting Our Widows and Widowers in Retirement Act (No bill): Proposals to improve benefits for widows and widowers in two-income households. The Surviving Widow(er) Income Fair Treatment Act (SWIFT Act) (S. 3255/H.R. 9763): Proposal to increase survivors benefits for disabled widows, widowers, and surviving divorced spouses; Social Security Enhancement and Protection Act (H.R. 3517): Proposal would improve Social Security benefits by increasing the Special Minimum Benefit, boosting benefits for seniors who have on the Social Security rolls for a long period of time, restore student benefits to age 26 and extend the life of the Trust Funds by eliminating the cap on Social Security benefits and phasing-in an increase in the payroll tax rate. The Social Security Survivor Benefits Equity Act (H.R. 6424/S. 3357): Proposal to increase the lump-sum benefit amount payable upon the death of a beneficiary to take into account inflation. Social Security Funding. The Medicare and Social Security Fair Share Act (H.R. 3271/S. 1690): Proposals to close the loophole for wealthy individuals who bypass paying the net investment income tax (NIIT) and directing the revenue to the Social Security Trust Funds and to the Hospital Insurance Fund, which pays for Medicare Part A that covers inpatient care in hospitals. Cutting Social Security by Raising the Retirement Age. Affirming the Presidents Promise Not to Raise the Social Security and Medicare Retirement Age (H. Res. 657): House Resolution opposing raising Social Security or Medicare eligibility age. Caregiver Social Security Credits. The Social Security Caregiver Credits Act (S. 4396/H.R. 8490): Proposal to provide Social Security wage credits for individuals who reduce their participation in the workforce or leave the workforce to provide care to specified family members and relatives. Social Security Notch. (No bill): Proposals to ensure that Social Security benefits for individuals born in 1960 and 1961 are not reduced as a result of the coronavirus-related drop in the average wage index. Protecting Seniors from Garnishment. Stop Social Security Garnishment Act of 2026 (S. 5456/H.R. 3967), Protection of Social Security Benefits Restoration Act (S. 5532/H.R. 10557): Proposals to protect Social Security beneficiaries from having their Social Security benefits garnished to recover unpaid student loans. Social Security Disability Insurance Claim Adjudication. (No bill): Proposal to nullify the rule finalized by the Social Security Administration on November 16, 2020, that outlines when its administrative appeals judges may hold hearings and issue decisions on individual cases. Currently, these judges serve an appellate function where they review, at the request of Social Security claimants, the decisions of the administrative law judges who issue decisions in individual cases. Social Security Overpayments. (H.R. 2999, H.R. 2142 and S. 1023): Proposals to protect retirees, survivors and people with disabilities from being forced to repay extra Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits they received through no fault of their own. Strengthening Beneficiaries Rights. (No bill): Various proposals relating to the protection and rights available to Social Security and Supplemental Security Income beneficiaries. Social Security Benefit Statements. The Know Your Social Security Act (No bill): Proposal to implement section 1143 of the Social Security Act by clarifying the Social Security Administration is required to mail annual benefit statements to all workers over age 25. Supplemental Security Income (SSI) Program. The Supplemental Security Income Restoration Act (S. 4001/H.R. 7828): Proposals to strengthen and restore the SSI program. Supplemental Security Income (SSI) Program. The SSI Savings Penalty Elimination Act (H.R. 2540/S. 1234): Proposal to amend title XVI of the Social Security Act to update the resource limit for Supplemental Security Income eligibility. The Fairness in Social Security Act (No bill): Proposal to amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to exclude the portion of a lump-sum Social Security benefit payment that relates to periods prior to the taxable year from the determination of household income as it relates to SSI eligibility. Retirement Plan Distribution: IRS Notice relating to Use of an Electronic Medium to Make Participant Elections and Spousal Consents (RIN 1545-Bq50). House Committee on Aging. (H. Res. 1013): A Resolution amending the Rules of the House to reestablish a Permanent Select Committee on Aging. Retirement Plan Fiduciary Rule: U.S. Department of Labor, Employee Benefits Security Administration, Office of Regulations and Interpretations - RIN 1210-AC02; Application No. D-12057; Application No. D-12060. The Department of Labor proposed regulation to modernize the fiduciary rule to strengthen protections for retirement investors who seek professional investment advice. (No bill): Congressional reversal of the rule submitted by the Department of Labor relating to "Retirement Security Rule: Definition of an Investment Advice Fiduciary". Retirement Plan Investment Alternatives: U.S. Department of Labor, Employee Benefits Security Administration, RIN 1210-AC38. Submitted comments opposing a proposed regulation defining Fiduciary Duties in Selecting Designated Investment Alternatives in 401(k) and other defined contribution plans. Proposal would create safe harbors for fiduciaries who select the investment options offered in 401(k) plans. If a fiduciary considers six factors when selecting any investment option, including alternative assets such as private equity, private credit, real estate, or cryptocurrency to a plan menu, the proposal would treat the fiduciary as meeting ERISAs prudence standard with respect to those factors, which would entitle the fiduciary to deference from any reviewing court. A bill that would undermine ERISAs ability to protect retirement plan participants hard-earned retirement income under the erroneous notion that the recent unanimous Supreme Court decision in Cunningham v. Cornell University will lead to a tide of ERISA class action litigation. Social Security Administration. Proposals to reverse cuts the Trump Administration has made to the Social Security Administration (SSA), prevents Social Security field offices from shutting down, makes it easier for seniors and people with disabilities to apply for the benefits they have earned over the phone, provides the resources the SSA needs to approve earned benefits quickly, protects benefits from unauthorized tampering, delays or changes, blocks privatization of SSA, enforces privacy protections for beneficiary data, and requires annual Government Accountability Office audits on staffing, operations and compliance. Social Security Administration. Letter to Social Security Commissioner Frank Bisignano opposing enhanced identity verification procedures for beneficiary transactions with SSA that will make it difficult, if not impossible, for many older Americans and members of the disability community to access their earned benefits. Social Security Administration. Resolution of Inquiry by Representative John Larson (H. Social Security Administration. Keep Our Field Offices Open Act (H.R. 1876): Proposals to suspend Social Security field office closures until January 21, 2029, after which date the Commissioner of Social Security would be required to submit a detailed report to Congress, laying out and justifying a process for closing, consolidating, or reducing access to field offices; bill also requires the Commissioner to maintain the total number of field offices and hearing offices that were in operation on January 20, 2025, after the moratorium ends and requires that, in considering future office closures, the Commissioner must consider potential transportation and communication barriers for individuals served by the office, provide significant advance notice to the public and members of Congress, and ensure opportunities for public input and appeals. Social Security Administration. Protecting Americans Social Security Data Act (H.R. 1877): Proposals to protect Americans from having their sensitive personal information politicized or bought and sold to the highest bidder by preventing Elon Musk, his associates, and political appointees from accessing sensitive data systems at SSA, codifying SSA data privacy requirements into law and strengthening oversight and civil penalties for any privacy and disclosure violations of Social Security beneficiaries personal information. Social Security Administration. The Improving Social Securitys Service to Victims of Identity Theft Act (S. 1666/H.R. 5345): Proposal to improve Social Security's service to victims of identity theft by requiring the Social Security Administration to provide a single point of contact for any individual whose Social Security account number has been misused.
